terms.gloss: favour, goodwill; one’s standing with others
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.14.7: cum aliquō in grātiam redīre (Lewis & Short)
Caes. BG 1.9.3: grātiā et largītiōne … plūrimum poterat
terms.comment: Both the favour one finds with others and the influence it brings: in grātiā esse cum aliquō, be on good terms with someone; in grātiam redīre, make it up; grātiam inīre ab aliquō, win someone’s favour (Lewis & Short). Its other common senses are a favour done (see favour, a kindness), thanks (grātiās agere) and, in poetry and later prose, charm.
The goodwill one person feels for another, on which friendship rests; most frequent in Cicero (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Fam. 5.8.4: eximium et singulāre meum studium (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: First zeal, eagerness, and the pursuit or study of something; of persons, devoted support, and so partisanship (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Sest. 115: quī favōre populī tenētur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Rare in Cicero, who apologised for it as a new word, and not in Caesar; frequent from Augustus on, especially of the favour of the people or of a crowd at the games (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: favour, be well disposed to, support

phrases.latin: est enim amīcitia nihil aliud nisi omnium dīvīnārum hūmānārumque rērum cum benevolentiā et cāritāte cōnsēnsiō
phrases.english: for friendship is nothing else than agreement on all things divine and human, with goodwill and affection

phrases.latin: amīcōs sublevāte; miserīs parcite; bonīs favēte
phrases.english: help your friends; spare the wretched; favour the good
